candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 30 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 31 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 32 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 33 not required. 34

candidates.statement: HABP/VABP trials should be randomized and double-blind when possible, comparing the 111 investigational drug with an active control. In general, HABP/VABP trials will be designed as 112 noninferiority trials. Another trial design is the add-on superiority design, in which patients 113 receive either a placebo or an investigational drug added to standard-of-care antibacterial drug 114 therapy. 115

For an indication for the treatment of HABP/VABP, the trial population should consist of 119 patients who have HABP (regardless of mechanical ventilation) or VABP. The trial population 120 should include at a minimum approximately 50 percent of patients who are on mechanical 121 ventilation at enrollment (VABP/ventilated HABP). Sponsors interested in seeking an indication 122 for HABP only should discuss the trial design and trial population with the Agency. 123
candidates.context: The protocol can specify the use of a clinical severity scoring system to identify a trial 125 population consisting of patients who have a sufficient severity of illness to maintain assay 126 sensitivity for the all-cause mortality endpoint in a noninferiority trial (e.g., at least a 15 percent 127 mortality rate). An example of a clinical severity scoring system is the Acute Physiology and 128 Chronic Health Evaluation II. 129

candidates.statement: Sponsors should consider methods to enhance the efficiency of the enrollment and randomization 189 processes and enable prompt administration of antibacterial drug therapy within the context of 190 the clinical trial, thus avoiding the potential confounding by effective antibacterial drug therapy 191 before enrollment (see section III. B. 8., Prior Antibacterial Drug Therapy). For example, it 192 often may be the case that few HABP/VABP patients are enrolled at each clinical center. In this 193 case, sponsors may consider randomizing centers rather than individual patients to simplify 194 enrollment, with appropriate adjustments to the statistical analysis plan and informed consent 195 procedures to accommodate cluster randomization. As another example, sponsors could give 196 hospitalized patients at risk for developing HABP/VABP informed consent in anticipation of 197 participating in a clinical trial if the patient develops HABP/VABP (Corneli et al. 2018). 198

candidates.statement: The trials should include patients of both sexes, patients of all races, and geriatric patients. 10 The 202 FDA encourages sponsors to begin discussions about their pediatric formulation and clinical 203 development plan early in development because pediatric studies are a required part of the 204 overall drug development program and sponsors are required to submit pediatric study plans no 205 later than 60 days after an end-of-phase 2 meeting. 11 Extrapolation of adult efficacy findings in 206 HABP/VABP to pediatrics is generally acceptable. However, studies are typically needed to 207 determine the appropriate dose and assess the safety of the drug in the pediatric population. 208 Sponsors should evaluate the pharmacokinetic (PK) information of the drug in specific 209 populations (e.g., geriatric patients, patients with renal or hepatic impairment) to determine 210 whether dose adjustments are necessary. 211

candidates.statement: To choose the dose or doses to be evaluated in phase 3 clinical trials, sponsors should integrate 215 the findings from nonclinical toxicology studies; animal models of infection; pharmacokinetics, 216 safety, and tolerability information from phase 1 clinical trials; and safety and efficacy 217 information from phase 2 dose-ranging clinical trials. Trials assessing drug penetration at the 218 site of action (e.g., epithelial lining fluid) may be helpful in defining doses that achieve 219 concentrations sufficient to exert an antibacterial effect. 220

candidates.statement: The active comparator drug should reflect the current standard of care for the treatment of 227 HABP/VABP. When evaluating the current standard of care, the FDA considers the 228 recommendations by authoritative scientific bodies (e.g., American Thoracic Society, Infectious 229 Diseases Society of America) based on clinical evidence and other reliable information that 230 reflects current clinical practice. 231
candidates.context: 7. Choice of Comparators and Concomitant Antibacterial Drugs 225 Ideally, an investigational drug would have activity against most bacterial pathogens implicated 233 in HABP/VABP and concomitant antibacterial drugs would not be necessary. However, 234 investigational drugs with a narrow spectrum of antibacterial activity can be developed for the 235 treatment of HABP/VABP. Because concomitant antibacterial drugs can confound the 236

candidates.statement: interpretation of treatment effect in a noninferiority trial, the protocol should specify any use of 237 concomitant antibacterial drugs that may be permitted for treating patients with HABP/VABP 238 and address the impact these concomitant drugs may have on study conclusions. 239

candidates.statement: Sponsors should discuss with the Agency the prespecified primary analysis population before 341 initiating the trial. In general, it is acceptable to consider the ITT population as the primary 342 analysis population. For antibacterial drugs with a narrow spectrum of activity (e.g., a drug 343 active against a single genus and species of bacteria), the micro-ITT population will be 344 considered the primary analysis population. 345
candidates.context: • Per-protocol microbiologically evaluable populations — Patients who are characterized 337 in the per-protocol population and have a baseline bacterial pathogen identified as the 338 cause of HABP/VABP. 339 b. Noninferiority margins 347

candidates.statement: Historical data support the appropriateness of noninferiority trials for HABP/VABP (see the 349 Appendix). For example, with the use of a survival endpoint, a noninferiority margin of 10 350 percent can be supported by the historical evidence, which supports a reduction in mortality by 351 effective therapy of about 20 percent. A 10 percent noninferiority margin supports a 352 preservation of a meaningful fraction of that effect. If a noninferiority margin >10 percent is 353 selected, sponsors should discuss the rationale and justification with the Agency. 354

candidates.statement: Sponsors should obtain blood samples from patients in phase 2 and phase 3 clinical trials (sparse 378 sampling) to estimate drug exposure in each patient. Sponsors should perform an exposure- 379 response analysis for clinical outcomes, microbiologic outcomes, and clinically relevant adverse 380 events. If phase 3 trials include a previously unstudied specific population, such as patients with 381 renal or hepatic impairment, collecting plasma drug concentrations from those specific 382 populations can aid in determining necessary dose adjustments. 383
